title: how to play social chess
summary: This video explains social chess, which involves using psychology to make the most of social interactions. The main lesson is that you can influence social outcomes by asking better questions, stating points early, following through, restating what others say, and making concrete invitations.
key_points: To make people like talking to you, give them a follow-up question because people want to be perceived as interesting and like when you are interested in them.
If you want people to listen to you, give your point early instead of minutes of background information.
If you want people to feel understood, restate what they said and check if you actually understood them after they finish explaining or telling a story.
To make people trust you, follow through on small things like sending things that interest them or sending little thank-you notes.
To make people think you care, follow up on what they tell you, such as milestones or dates, by writing a note and sending a message.
To turn an acquaintance into a friend, make your invitations super concrete by giving a day, time, activity, and location so it is easy to say yes or no.
content:
how to play social chess

I'm going to teach you how to play social chess. What is it? Well, social chess is all about using other people's psychology to make the most out of the social interactions that you're having. So I'm going to be telling you that if this is what you want from a social interaction, then this is how you're going to get it. 

If you want people to like talking to you, give them a follow-up question. Because what people want is to be perceived as interesting. If somebody thinks that you are interested in them, they are going to like talking to you much, much more. And the way that you generate that feeling is by asking very specific questions about what it is that they're telling you, so that it shows that you're listening and that you care. 

If you want people to listen to you, give your point early. No one wants to hear minutes and minutes of background information. They want to hear specifically what it is that you think. There are differences in linguistic style, and people often perceive people from Germany or from Scandinavia as much better at doing this. 

If you want people to feel understood, which is the best way of developing deep interpersonal connection, then check whether you've actually understood them. After they've finished explaining something or after they've finished telling you a story, repeat it back to them summarized, and check whether this understanding is correct. What you're doing is you're giving people a chance to explain what really matters out of what it is that they've told you. 

If you want people to trust you, you need to be following through on the small things. It's not just showing up when you say that you're going to show up. It's things like actually sending them things that you think that would interest them, or it's sending them little thank-you notes after they've done something nice for you or hosted you. You want to be giving people repeated experiences of your words actually matching your actions. 

If you want people to think that you care, you need to be following up on what it is that they tell you. If they tell you about a particular milestone or a date that's important to them, write a little note about it after that conversation, because otherwise you are going to forget it, your working memory has very limited capacity. And on that date or at that milestone, send them a message. Remind them that you are thinking about them. 

If you want an acquaintance to become a friend, make your invitation super concrete. Give them a day, give them a time, give them something to do, somewhere to go. It becomes very, very easy to say yes or no to that when there is specificity. If everything is very vague, "do you want to hang out at some point?", then that makes it very, very hard to actually arrange something. 

So social chess is all about using psychology to think one move ahead in social situations. And if you found that interesting, you'll love the rest of my content too.
